fields.expected:
Most of what I've built over the past two years has been about agents that touch real workflows, and specifically about where they should stop. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript that moves every application through an explicit state machine, keeps SQLite as the single source of truth because browser state diverging across processes is how agents do damage, and puts every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. I also built a validation ladder so a capability isn't called working until it's confirmed against the level of reality it claims to support, not just a local fixture.

That is basically the problem Sierra is solving at production scale: agents that act on behalf of real companies with real customers, where a wrong action is a real consequence. At Intelehealth I evaluated LLM outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, which convinced me that generation is cheap and deciding whether to trust output is the hard part. I'd want to work on agent evaluation and reliability, and Craftsmanship as a stated value is why I want it to be here.

fields.expected:
The engineers I'd trust with agents are the ones who treat evaluation as the hard part. Generating an output with an LLM is cheap; deciding whether it should be trusted is where the work is. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case benchmark, using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes rather than reporting an average score. That changed how I build. In my job-application agent I wrote a validation ladder, UNIT_CONFIRMED to FIXTURE_CONFIRMED to LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, because a capability passing a local fixture is not a capability that works against a real ATS.

The second quality is knowing where the agent should hand back to a person. Free-text and demographic fields in that system are architecturally prevented from autofill and always generate a human review item. In tSearch, missing evidence returns "insufficient evidence" instead of a low score.

I'm an undergraduate, not a senior engineer, but I've shipped systems people actually used, including an iOS app in a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, and I change my design when reality contradicts it.

fields.expected: Two things that didn't fit elsewhere. First, I ship things and then have to convince people they should exist. I built ClarityAtlas end to end in Swift and SwiftUI, including a passive sleep-estimation system using HealthKit and Core Motion signals so users wouldn't need a wearable, and got it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users. The harder part was everything around it: recruiting users, getting into NSF I-Corps and the Pava Spark Accelerator, and pitching President Daniels after my cofounders and I knocked on the doors of Garland Hall until someone let us in. Second, I spend a lot of time on a question that I think is relevant to agent work even though it started somewhere else. Over the past year I studied how research institutions decide which uncertain work gets funded, and interviews kept pushing me toward the same conclusion: as generation gets cheap, judgment becomes the scarce resource. That is the same reason I care about evaluation harnesses and human-review gates rather than more autonomy by default. I'm targeting Winter 2027 and happy to be in San Francisco in person.
